tone_statements.citation: Bernot, Denise. 2008. Trying to Trace Back Tones in Burmese. Moussons: Recherche en sciences humaines sur l'Asie du Sud-Est 12: 173-185. Aix-en-Provence: Presses Universitaires de Provence.
tone_statements.quote: After a period of fluctuation, in the early 12 th c., the syllables regularly written with final h as well as with final vowel carrier a in old Burmese, most of the time have respectively nowadays breathy and creaky tone; while a continuum between long vowels or short vowels of old Burmese and, respectively, low tone and creaky tone of modern spoken Burmese is not regular, though noticeable: graphism of vowels was varying so much and so often in lithic or terracotta inscriptions that such a continuum could not be expected.
tone_statements.locator: paragraph 75 (part IV, conclusion; pp. 173-185, paragraph numbering of the OpenEdition HTML); see also paragraphs 2 and 20-41 on the OB marks
tone_statements.summary: OB writing shows a three-way marking on open rhymes (short V / long V / long V + h) and -' vs zero on e- and nasal rhymes, ancestral to modern creaky / low / breathy; whether these were already pitch tones in the 12th c. is left open.

tone_statements.citation: Ohno, Toru. 2005. The structure of Pagan period Burmese. In Justin Watkins (ed.), Studies in Burmese Linguistics (Pacific Linguistics 570), 241-305. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-570.241; hdl 1885/254240.
tone_statements.quote: [p. 250] Burmese of the Pagan period is thought to have been tonal, as is modem Burmese. Tones are sometimes represented during the earlier stage of the Pagan period by the addition of partIcular symbols: [...] _a corresponds to modem Burmese creaky tone. [...] correspond frequently, but not consistently, to low and high tones, respectively, as in the examples in (20). [...] [p. 301] The vowels were a i U e 0 ; the diphthongs seem to have been ai and ui. [...] It is generally agreed that three tones were distinguished.
tone_statements.summary: Three tones (creaky / low / high, matching the modern system) assumed for Pagan-period Burmese; orthographic marking partial and inconsistent: -a for creaky (early period only), vowel-length symbols and final -h loosely for low vs high.

tone_statements.citation: Nishi, Yoshio. 1997 [issue dated 1998-03-31]. The Orthographic Standardization of Burmese: Linguistic and Sociolinguistic Speculations [ビルマ語(ミャンマー語)綴字法の標準化: 言語学的, 社会言語学的考察]. Bulletin of the National Museum of Ethnology (国立民族学博物館研究報告) 22(4): 975-999. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology.
tone_statements.quote: What is significant about the former system to the history of Burmese is that it undoubtedly attests that there were three distinctive tones in OB as early as the twelfth century and perhaps before. [...] Thus, it is clear that there were already three distinctive tones even before OB, and they have remained distinctive since. The problem remains, however, what the nature of tonal distinction in OB is. The fact that tones 2 and 3 are graphically represented by -h/-h and -', respectively, the latter perhaps indicating a glottal stop or laryngealization, may be interpreted to suggest that the distinctive features of these tones were voice registers rather than pitches in the earlier stage of Burmese.
tone_statements.locator: p. 986 and p. 988, section 2 (first standardization in the OB period); see also n. 15, p. 993
tone_statements.summary: Old Burmese: 3 contrastive tones on open/nasal rhymes (T1 unmarked/long vowel, T2 written -h/visarga, T3 written -' or short vowel) + stop-final checked rhymes (= modern T4); contrasts probably phonation-register based (breathy, creaky/glottal) shifting to pitch within the OB period.

tone_statements.citation: 汪大年 [Wang Danian]. 1986. 妙齐提碑文研究(一)——十二世纪初缅甸语音初探 [A study of the Myazedi inscription (1): a first look at early-12th-century Burmese phonology]. 北京大学学报(哲学社会科学版) 1986(4): 103-118 as printed in the journal PDF (the journal-site/CNKI metadata gives 105-120).
tone_statements.quote: 在“妙齐提”碑文时期，只有元音长短之分还没有高平调出现，如果说，元音长短区别音位，可把它们算作声调。那么当时只有两个声调，一个短调，一个长调。妙碑中反映出来在古缅语中，有着较丰富的声母系统和辅音韵尾系统，因而声调的区别作用幷不突出，字音的高低变化，只是一种伴随特征。幷不具备音位功能。[p.117:] 关于声调，我们的结论是：古缅语中只有长、短两调。后来的四个声调是历史发展的结果。[a']尾、[h]尾是分别表示短调和长调的一种符号。
tone_statements.translation: In the period of the Myazedi inscription there was only a distinction of vowel length; no high-level tone had yet appeared. If one takes vowel length as phonemically distinctive, one may count them as tones; then there were only two tones at the time, a short tone and a long tone. As the inscription shows, Old Burmese had a fairly rich system of initials and consonant codas, so the distinguishing role of tone was not prominent; variation in the pitch of syllables was only a concomitant feature and had no phonemic function. ... On tone, our conclusion is: Old Burmese had only two 'tones', long and short. The later four tones are the result of historical development. Final [a'] and final [h] are symbols marking the short and the long tone respectively.
tone_statements.locator: p. 116, section 三 声调 + p. 117, section 四 结语
tone_statements.summary: Author posits only a long vs short vowel-length '调' contrast, pitch explicitly non-phonemic; coded as no tone. One could instead record 2 length 'tones' (短调, 长调). Argued from inscription spellings.

sources.locator: p. 986 and p. 988, section 2 (first standardization in the OB period); see also n. 15, p. 993
sources.note: OB was a tone language with three distinctive tones for non-stop rhymes already in the 12th c. (and before OB, by Lolo-Burmese correspondences); inscriptions mark tone 1 by long vowel symbols, tone 2 by -h / visarga, tone 3 by -' (glottal stop/laryngealization) or short vowel symbols; the Asawlat (1165) system distinguishes all three; stop-final rhymes correspond to modern tone 4; Nishi hypothesises the OB contrasts were phonation registers (breathy for tone 2, creaky/glottal for tone 3) with tone 2 vs 1 shifting to pitch during the OB period, implying a later tonal flip-flop.
